competitors.name: Splitwise
competitors.model: Freemium with a metered free tier. Splitwise Pro in-app purchases listed on the US App Store are $2.99, $3.99, $4.99, $29.99 and $39.99 (monthly and annual tiers; secondary sources report $4.99/mo and $39.99/yr). Free tier has a daily expense cap plus full-screen ads.
competitors.note: The category incumbent and the name people search, 3.95/5 from 26,928 US iOS ratings, which is remarkably low for a market leader and is almost entirely monetization damage. The decisive fact for us is what sits behind the paywall: splitwise.com/pro lists 'Unlimited expenses', 'Currency conversion', 'Receipt scanning', 'Itemization', 'Expense search', 'Charts and graphs', 'Default split settings' and an ad-free experience as Pro-only. Itemization, the single thing a restaurant bill splitter is for, is a paid feature at the market leader. Splitwise's own knowledgebase confirms 'Splitwise has introduced a daily expense limit for our free tier' and suggests you 'wait for the daily limit to reset' or ask 'a friend to add the expenses on your behalf.' Strongest at: network effect, cross-platform sync, long-running roommate ledgers. Soft spot: the moment of use is exactly the moment they interrupt you.

competitors.name: tricount (by bunq)
competitors.model: Free and ad-free core, owned by Dutch neobank bunq since 2022; monetized by funnelling users toward a bunq account and a 'free' bunq card in the app. IAPs present.
competitors.note: The strongest free competitor by rating, 4.875/5 from 6,616 US iOS ratings, and its own store copy claims 'over 17 million users' with bills 'free and unlimited.' Ad-free, multi-currency, receipt scanning, dark mode. Two soft spots, both visible in its 1-star reviews. First, people do not trust the arithmetic: 'App has the total expenses correct but every other amount is wrong', 'The calculations are just very basically wrong', 'The Math is completely wrong and I can't figure out how to fix it.' Second, the product is a bank's acquisition funnel, the card tab and bunq linkage are the business model, which means the incentive is to move you into a financial relationship, not to end your evening quickly.

competitors.name: Splid
competitors.model: Free, no sign-up, no ads for the core product; IAPs exist (one-time unlocks per group/user rather than a subscription).
competitors.note: 4.91/5 from 3,901 US iOS ratings, the highest-rated app in the category and the closest thing to our philosophy that ships in an app store: no account, works offline, free currency conversion across 150+ currencies. This is the app to study, not dismiss. Its structural weakness is the one Kittysplit attacks in its own comparison page: Splid is 'iOS and Android only. There's no browser version', so every participant must install something. Ours opens from a link on any phone at the table, including the friend with a locked-down work device. Splid also carries the same trust crack: 'Calculations are WRONG!!! … don't rely on it to do the math at the end, because someone will get ripped off!!'

competitors.name: Settle Up (Step Up Labs)
competitors.model: Free with ads; Premium (lifetime purchase, plus newer time-boxed 'Group Premium' packages and a 7-day trial on the yearly tier) removes ads and unlocks receipt photos, categories, recurring transactions, receipt sync and Excel export.
competitors.note: 4.82/5 from 1,687 US iOS ratings, and the developer publishes his monetization openly, which makes him a very quotable source. His own 2025 write-up states free users get a fullscreen ad 'after every 3rd expense added', preceded by a feature-promotion screen 'inspired by Instagram Stories design', and reports the trial change produced '1.8× revenue on Android and 1.9× revenue on iOS.' That is the whole category business model stated in the first person: the ad fires precisely when you are mid-task. Strongest at: recurring expenses and long-lived shared-house ledgers, which we deliberately do not do.

competitors.name: Kittysplit
competitors.model: Browser-first, no registration, no password. Free for groups up to 9 people; a one-time 'Super Kitty' upgrade of roughly €3 per group (not per person) unlocks 10+ members, multiple currencies and receipt uploads. Free CSV export.
competitors.note: Our nearest strategic neighbour and the competitor most people have never heard of, 'Splitting bills since 2012. In any browser, no app required.' It has already won the argument we are making (no install, share a link, everyone participates) and it prices honestly: one small fee for the whole group rather than per-head. Exploitable soft spots: the paywall lands exactly where a group gets interesting (the 10th person, and any second currency, the two things a real holiday needs), and the event lives on their server behind a secret URL, so 'no account' is not the same as 'nothing leaves your device.' We are free at 10 people, free in two currencies, and genuinely local.

competitors.name: Tab (bring10, LLC)
competitors.model: Free, no login required for friends, camera-based receipt OCR.
competitors.note: 4.22/5 from 1,136 US iOS ratings and the app people mean when they say 'just scan the receipt.' It is the best evidence in this whole file that OCR is a marketing feature, not a working one: 'Captured only 2 of 15 items', 'hallucinating money', 'horrible at scanning… have to enter manually', 'the numbers it pulls is crazy sometimes', 'The tax button is broken and you cannot calculate the correct amount', 'no ability to add tax manually.' It also expires your work, 'bills auto delete after just a couple of weeks', 'Can't edit bills after 1 week', and refuses uploaded images: 'you can only use if you take a photo of the receipt. You cannot upload a previous photo.' Fast, correct manual entry beats a scanner that needs correcting.

competitors.name: Plates by Splitwise
competitors.model: Genuinely free, no account, no ads, no IAP. Effectively abandonware, shipped 2013, unchanged since.
competitors.note: 4.34/5 from 922 US iOS ratings for a thirteen-year-old app, which tells you how badly the category serves the restaurant-table moment. Its drag-an-item-onto-a-plate interaction is still the best in the category and worth stealing conceptually. Its failures are all fixable-by-us: percentage-only tip with no manual amount ('please add manual tip amount + names', 'Not flexible enough to be useful'), plates are anonymous so you cannot tell who is who past three people, a 10-person ceiling, forced landscape orientation ('impossible to flip between other apps'), and no way out of the app with your result. Splitwise has no incentive to revive it, itemization is now a Pro feature of the paid product.

competitors.name: Venmo Groups / Cash App / PayPal built-ins
competitors.model: Free to use; monetized on the payment rail (instant-transfer fees, ~3% credit-card surcharge).
competitors.note: Venmo launched Groups in November 2023, 'one of our most requested features', supporting up to 32 people per group and 20 groups per user, with no paywall. This is the existential competitor: it is free, it is where the money actually moves, and it needs no second app. But it is US-only, it requires every participant to hold a Venmo account with real identity verification, it does not do itemized restaurant splitting with tax and tip apportioned per dish, and it is a payment network, it wants the transaction. We are the calculator that hands off to it. Positioning against Venmo is 'work out the number correctly, then pay however you already pay', not 'instead of Venmo.'

competitors.name: The zero-app default: phone calculator, Google Sheets, and free tip-splitter web pages
competitors.note: The real market share holder, and a Splitwise 1-star review says it out loud: 'Just use a Google sheet… understanding the debts feels more complicated than if you just used a Google sheet, and you can only put a couple items in there before it caps you.' Divide-by-four on the calculator app is the true incumbent for a four-person dinner, and it wins on zero friction and total trust, you saw the arithmetic. It loses the moment tax, tip, one person's cocktails, and 'who pays whom' collide. Our job is to be as instantly trustworthy as a calculator while doing the part a calculator can't, which is why showing the working is a strategy and not a nicety.

complaints.complaint: The market leader meters the single action the app exists for, and makes you watch an ad to perform it. Verbatim 1-star reviews: 'You have to watch a 10 second video before you can enter an expense and you're limited to 3 entries per day' (Rachel4450). 'With a daily limit of 3 expenses this app is useless unless you are willing to pay' (Yippyipp2). 'you can only add so many expenses at once until the Pro pops up tries to charge you, is RIDICULOUS' (LoMo48). 'Tried to add a third expense mid-trip and they started demanding money' (Everything ees taken). 'Making me wait 10s is so lame… let's waste our customers time to get them to upgrade to pro' (IlIlIjjjjx). Settle Up's developer describes the same mechanic in his own words: a fullscreen ad 'after every 3rd expense added.'
complaints.source: Apple's public customer-reviews RSS feed for Splitwise (itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=458023433), verbatim, most-recent reviews, read directly; Splitwise's own knowledgebase article 'Why am I seeing an expense limit?' (feedback.splitwise.com/knowledgebase/articles/2010350) confirming 'Splitwise has introduced a daily expense limit for our free tier'; medium.com/step-up-labs 'Summary of 2025 changes in monetization of Settle Up'
complaints.weWinIf: There is no counter and no interstitial anywhere, and we say so in the place competitors put a pricing table. Concretely: adding a person, an item or an expense must never be gated, delayed, animated, or followed by anything. The tip jar stays a footer link, never a button on the add path, and never a modal. The design rule that follows: nothing may ever appear over the add-expense control, and the add button must not move after a successful add, that is precisely where the incumbents put the ad.

complaints.complaint: Itemization, splitting a restaurant bill by dish, is a paid feature at the market leader. splitwise.com/pro lists 'Itemization', 'Currency conversion', 'Receipt scanning', 'Expense search', 'Charts and graphs' and 'Default split settings' as Pro-only. Kittysplit charges its ~€3 upgrade for 'multiple currencies' and groups past 9 people. Settle Up charges for receipt photos, categories and Excel export.
complaints.source: splitwise.com/pro (fetched directly); kittysplit.com/en/splid-alternative (Kittysplit's own comparison page, stating free up to 9 people, ~€3 one-time per group for 10+ members, multi-currency and receipt uploads); medium.com/step-up-labs Settle Up monetization post
complaints.weWinIf: We publish a negative-space list where they publish a pricing table, and every line is a real gated feature named by a real competitor: itemized by-dish splitting, free. Any number of people, free. A second currency, free. Every expense, free. No ads, no countdown, no card on file, no account. Our build already ships itemization (index.html:2091 renderItems) and per-expense currency conversion (index.html:1337-1352); the failure would be not saying so.

complaints.complaint: Nobody trusts the arithmetic, and this is the deepest wound in the whole category. tricount 1-star: 'We have a fairly simple list of expenses: 5 people, 15 entries. App has the total expenses correct but every other amount is wrong.' 'This one particular person should have a split $25 + $52 = $77 but the app was showing the person owing me around $96.32.' 'The calculations are just very basically wrong.' Splid 1-star: 'Calculations are WRONG!!! … It's a good tool for keeping track of who spent what & who was involved, but don't rely on it to do the math at the end, because someone will get ripped off!!' Tab 1-star: 'hallucinating money', 'Subtotal page adds unexplained amounts.'
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feeds read directly: tricount id=349866256, Splid id=991473495, Tab id=595068606
complaints.weWinIf: This is the biggest opening in the category and it is a pure design job: SHOW THE WORKING. Every person's figure must expand into the derivation that produced it, 'Steak 34.00 ÷ 2 = 17.00, half the calamari 6.25, share of tax 2.41, share of tip 4.02 → 29.68', and every results card must carry a visible reconciliation line proving the parts sum to the whole ('4 shares · 118.40 · exactly the bill total'). Our math is already right (integer cents throughout, largest-remainder allocation at index.html:1495-1520, unit-tested), so we are the only app that can afford to open the box. In a category where the top complaint is 'the numbers are wrong', being auditable is worth more than any feature.

complaints.complaint: The settle-up result arrives with no explanation of what it is for, which makes it socially unusable. tricount 1-star, titled 'Missing most important feature': 'While it shows the balance of who owes what, it doesn't show any detail. It's impossible to ask for repayment without being able to answer "What for?"'
complaints.weWinIf: Every transfer carries its reason. Tapping 'Sam → Alex $41.20' expands into the expenses that produced it, and the Copy-summary and payment-link note both carry a human sentence ('Tahoe: your share of groceries 22.10, gas 12.60, cabin cleaning 6.50') rather than a bare figure. Our payButtons() at index.html:2122 already passes a note into the deep link, today it is just the trip name. Make it the reason. This directly serves the emotional problem below: people avoid asking because they cannot justify the number.

complaints.complaint: 'Fewest possible payments' is imposed with no alternative, and users want the plain version. tricount 3-star: 'I wish there was an option to see all debts without them being combined into the "least amount of transfers."' Related tricount 2-star: 'The app attempts to calculate a recommended way to split expenses and reimburse the group back, but it's not clear or easy to understand who has paid who back.' And 3-star: 'The app says person B owes person A $50. That is not correct. Once the balance of $50 is paid, person A has paid $50 and person B has paid $100.'
complaints.weWinIf: Offer two views of the same truth and let the group pick: 'Fewest payments' (our current settleUp() at index.html:1589) and 'Pay who you actually owe' (direct pairwise debts, no netting through a third party). Minimized settlement is mathematically elegant and socially confusing, it tells Sam to pay Priya, who Sam never ate with. VERIFIED GAP: index.html:2341 renderTripResults renders only the minimized set, under a heading that asserts it is the right answer.

complaints.complaint: Group ledgers break when someone settles early or edits a shared entry. Splitwise 1-star: 'Always messes up big groups, if someone settles up too early, it always messes things up… all the paywalls are ridiculous now.' Splitwise 3-star: 'if an expense is added by me in a group then other members should not be able to edit.' tricount 1-star: 'App includes the cost between people when it specifically shouldn't and that person isn't checked to be in the split.' tricount 2-star: 'you have to delete things manually and it notifies the other person even when you delete it.'
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feeds: Splitwise (id=458023433), tricount (id=349866256)
complaints.weWinIf: Two things. (1) Make payments first-class: you must be able to record 'Sam paid Alex $40 on Tuesday' as an event, so the ledger survives someone settling mid-trip. VERIFIED GAP, our state has no settlement record type at all (sanitizeState at index.html:1699 accepts only people, dinner and trip.expenses; there is no way to log a repayment, so a partially-settled trip cannot be represented). (2) Our single-editor model is a feature, not a limitation: one person holds the split and shares a snapshot, so nobody's entry silently changes under them. Say that plainly rather than apologising for the absence of sync.

complaints.complaint: Receipt OCR is the category's most-demanded and least-working feature. Tab 1-star reviews: 'Captured only 2 of 15 items' and incorrect pricing on the ones it did capture; 'only captures specific items and omits several others'; 'horrible at scanning… have to enter manually'; 'no matter how clear a screenshot is somehow it's still blurry'; 'Cannot upload images, Missing the most basic feature… you can only use if you take a photo of the receipt.' Meanwhile Plates users beg for it: 'No bill upload feature, Multiple meals? Tons of people/items on the order? Nightmare.'
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feeds: Tab (id=595068606), Plates by Splitwise (id=669801762)
complaints.weWinIf: We cannot do OCR on-device without breaking the no-upload promise, so we win by making manual entry faster than correcting a bad scan. That means: amount field focused on load, a numeric keypad, Enter commits and returns focus to the next amount, running subtotal visible as you type, and item name genuinely optional (it already is, index.html:1296). Target: eight items in under thirty seconds, one-handed. Then say why there is no camera, in one honest line, a scanner means an upload, and an upload means your receipt on someone's server.

complaints.complaint: Your ledger expires, or vanishes. Tab: 'bills auto delete after just a couple of weeks'; 'Can't edit bills after 1 week.' tricount users report groups disappearing and losing track of money owed. Splitwise gates 'Expense search' behind Pro, so finding an old split on the free tier means scrolling.
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feed, Tab (id=595068606); tricount complaints surfaced via search on together.bunq.com help-centre threads (secondary, not read in full); splitwise.com/pro feature list
complaints.weWinIf: Nothing expires and nothing is on a server that can lose it, but we must earn that claim, because our own storage story is currently invisible to the user. Our splits live in IndexedDB and in the URL hash with no visible save confirmation. Make persistence legible: a quiet 'Saved on this device' state, a Saved tab that shows date and total at a glance, and a one-tap export. Add CSV alongside the JSON export at index.html:2464, JSON is a developer's backup, a spreadsheet is a normal person's receipt, and Kittysplit gives CSV away free while Settle Up charges for Excel.

complaints.complaint: Tip handling is rigid and often mandatory. Plates 1-star: 'Not flexible enough to be useful', frustrated with the inability to enter custom tip amounts rather than percentages; 2-star 'Needs more' and 3-star 'please add manual tip amount + names' both ask for typed tip. Tab 1-star: 'Tips SUCK! Mandatory tip calculations SUCK!' and 2-star 'Not really simpler', forced tip on non-tippable expenses. Tab 4-star: tip calculation should factor tax; 'doesn't match standard tipping practices.'
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feeds: Plates by Splitwise (id=669801762), Tab (id=595068606)
complaints.weWinIf: We already have the %/$ toggle at index.html:1303, which is more than Plates has after thirteen years, but two things are missing. First, expose the choice of base: our tip is computed on the pre-tax subtotal only (index.html:1523 dinnerCompute, tip = subtotal × pct), which is the correct etiquette but not what many card readers do, and a user who cannot reconcile our number with their receipt will assume we are wrong. Add a visible 'on subtotal / on total' switch and show the resulting figure. Second, tip must be genuinely skippable with no nag, a trip expense for petrol should never suggest a tip.

complaints.complaint: The payment handoff is confusing and steered toward the vendor's own rail. Splitwise 2-star: 'Confusing to pay the split, payment choices are confusing and designed in a manipulated way', describing UI that directs users to bank connections rather than Venmo. Splitwise 2-star: 'Loyal user' asking for a 'payment platform agnostic' approach. Splitwise 1-star 'No longer useful' criticises the lack of Zelle 'despite years of requests.' Tab 2-star: 'venmo doesn't connect'; 1-star: Venmo connection fails.
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feed, Splitwise (id=458023433) and Tab (id=595068606)
complaints.weWinIf: We are structurally incapable of steering, because we never touch money, the README's hard rule. Make that visible: the payment row offers Venmo, Cash App and PayPal.me as equal-weight options with an always-present 'Copy amount' fallback for Zelle, cash, bank transfer or a bar tab, and no option is styled as the default. VERIFIED DEFECT: today those are the smallest controls in the app (payButtons at index.html:2122 renders sub-14px links in a .paybtns row), which is backwards, this is the terminal action of every flow and belongs at 44px minimum.

complaints.complaint: Splitting a bill should not require handing over identity. Splitwise's App Store privacy card declares that Name, Email Address, Phone Number, Coarse Location, User ID and Device ID are all linked to you, for both Analytics and App Functionality. One 1-star review: 'Account verification, Who has a Social Security card when they are traveling. Impossible to set up a new acct.' Another: 'Forces you to join. Forcing me into paid app.'
complaints.source: apps.apple.com/us/app/splitwise/id458023433 App Privacy section, read directly; Apple customer-reviews RSS feed, Splitwise (id=458023433)
complaints.weWinIf: State the negative claim as an object, not a sentence, and make it testable: no account, no email, no phone number, no location, no analytics, nothing uploaded, turn off Wi-Fi and it still works. But be honest about the one real leak we do have: a shared link carries the whole split, including any Venmo/Cash App/PayPal handles saved against a person, into whatever chat app it is pasted into. Say that at the Copy-link moment, not in a privacy page. Overclaiming here would be worse than the competitors' underclaiming.

complaints.complaint: Everyone at the table has to install the app and sign up, and the group tool collapses if one person won't. This is described across the category as the number-one adoption objection; Kittysplit builds its entire pitch on it ('In any browser, no app required'; with Splid, 'everyone must install the app'); Splid markets that not everyone from the group has to join; a whole app exists called 'OFFLINE Bill Splitter' whose stated origin is splitting bills 'without forcing friends to download the app or sign up.'
complaints.source: kittysplit.com/en/splid-alternative (Kittysplit's own comparison page, read directly); App Store listings for Splid (id=991473495) and OFFLINE Bill Splitter (id=1490112434); corroborated by category round-up articles
complaints.weWinIf: This is already our strongest structural advantage and it should be the headline, not a footnote. The link and QR carry the entire split, no install, no account, works on the one friend's ancient Android and the one with a locked work phone. Two upgrades: make the QR the primary share action at a restaurant table (it is the only one that works when you cannot type someone's number), and make 'Copy summary' produce a message that reads well pasted raw into a group chat, because that is what most people will actually do.

complaints.complaint: Free-tier subscriptions are hard to escape. Splitwise 1-star: 'We used once and cannot shut this off, Impossible to cancel - don't use.' 'Can't cancel subscription, Completely hidden cancellation, this needs to be easier.' 'DON'T, They ruined it. I used to spend a dollar or two for this app. These greedy insectile swine raised the price.' 'charging for this app is insane, used to be such a good app when it was free.' Splitwise 2-star: 'Not great if you need to cancel a payment… Trying to get my money back has been impossible.'
complaints.weWinIf: There is no payment surface in the product at all. The tip link must look like a link and read as post-hoc gratitude, never a CTA button, never on the results path, never with a price on it. Note this is the second-order damage of the incumbent's model: the loudest reviews are not about features, they are about feeling trapped. A visibly unmonetized tool is the emotional opposite, and that feeling is the product.

complaints.complaint: The result is trapped in the app. Plates 3-star: 'Where is the share button?', cannot locate sharing or see plate names in the summary. Plates 2-star asks for clearer export. Splitwise gates search and charts; Settle Up charges for Excel export; Splid offers no CSV at all (per Kittysplit's comparison). Splitwise 1-star: 'Overly complicated, A simple payment split turned into total chaos. Just use cash share app.'
complaints.source: Apple customer-reviews RSS feeds: Plates (id=669801762), Splitwise (id=458023433); kittysplit.com/en/splid-alternative
complaints.weWinIf: Four exits, all free, all one tap: a chat-ready text summary, a share link, a QR, and a printable/PDF sheet for the table. VERIFIED GAP: print styles exist (index.html:1101 and :1231) but there is no Print button anywhere in the UI, the share bar at index.html:1398 offers only Copy link, QR code and Copy summary. The printed sheet is exactly the artifact people put in the middle of a table, and we already render it; we just never offer it.

tableStakes: Assign individual items to individual people, with shared items split among a subset. WE HAVE IT, index.html:2091 renderItems, per-item person toggles, and items with nobody selected fall back to everyone (index.html:1523 dinnerCompute). This is Pro-only at Splitwise, so it is both a table stake and a headline.

Tax and tip apportioned proportionally to what each person actually ordered, not split evenly on top of an itemized bill. WE HAVE IT, dinnerCompute allocates tax+tip by each person's item subtotal via largest-remainder allocation (index.html:1495-1560).

Per-person shares that sum exactly to the bill, with no lost or invented pennies. WE HAVE IT, integer cents throughout, splitEven distributes the remainder, allocateProportional uses largest remainder; covered by test/unit.mjs. Given that 'the math is wrong' is the top complaint against tricount, Splid and Tab, this must also be VISIBLE, and today it is not.
Minimized settle-up: reduce N people's balances to the fewest transfers. WE HAVE IT, settleUp at index.html:1589, greedy, ≤ n−1 transfers.

Record a repayment, so a group that settles mid-trip stays correct. VERIFIED GAP IN OUR BUILD: there is no settlement or payment record anywhere. sanitizeState (index.html:1699) accepts only people, dinner and trip.expenses; an expense has {id,label,cents,currency,rate,baseCents,paidBy,split} and nothing else. renderTripResults (index.html:2341) recomputes transfers from expenses alone, so after Sam actually pays Alex the app keeps telling him to pay again. Splitwise, tricount and Settle Up all have this, and Splitwise's 'settles up too early' 1-star shows what happens when it is done badly. This is the single most important functional gap in the app.

Split by percentage, by shares, or by exact amount, not just evenly or by item. PARTIAL GAP: trip mode has weighted shares (the 'Uneven shares' checkbox at index.html:1337 feeding allocateProportional), but dinner mode offers only 'Split evenly' or 'By items' (index.html:1290-1300). There is no percentage mode and no exact-amount mode anywhere. Spliit lists 'percentage, shares, amount' as standard; a Splid reviewer asks for 'custom repayment percentages per person.'

Dates, notes and categories on an expense, enough context to find and justify an entry later. VERIFIED GAP: an expense is {id,label,cents,currency,rate,baseCents,paidBy,split} and nothing more (index.html:1760-1770), no date, no note, no category. Only the saved-split row carries a date, derived from updatedAt (index.html:2397). For a week-long trip with thirty expenses, 'when' is how people find the entry they are arguing about, and the label is currently the only place any 'what for' can live. Settle Up charges for categories; Spliit ships them free.

Multi-currency for a trip, with a per-expense rate. WE HAVE IT for trips (index.html:1341-1352, expCurrency/expRate/baseCents), a feature Splitwise puts behind Pro and Kittysplit behind its €3 upgrade. GAP: dinner mode has no currency control at all, so a bill split abroad shows dollar formatting unless the user first goes to the trip tab.

Exits a normal person can use: a spreadsheet export and a printable sheet. DOUBLE GAP: exportFile (index.html:2464) writes .split.json only, a developer's backup, not a receipt, while Kittysplit gives CSV away free and Settle Up sells Excel export. And print CSS exists at index.html:1101 and :1231 but no Print action exists anywhere; the share bar (index.html:1398) offers only Copy link, QR code and Copy summary. The printed settle-up sheet is exactly the artifact people put in the middle of a table, and we already render it, we just never offer it.

Undo, or at least a consistent confirmation, on every destructive action. VERIFIED GAP: deleting a saved split calls confirm() (index.html:2400-2404) but deleting an item, deleting an expense and removing a person are all immediate and irreversible, and there is no undo anywhere. The toast is already an aria-live region, so 'Expense deleted · Undo' is nearly free.

Works for people who install nothing and sign up for nothing. WE HAVE IT, the whole split is compressed into the URL hash and shareable by link or QR (index.html:1398 share bar), which is the thing Kittysplit built a company on and Splid structurally cannot do.

Hand off to how people actually pay, with a copy-the-number fallback. WE HAVE IT, payButtons at index.html:2122 emits Venmo, Cash App and PayPal.me deep links plus 'Copy amt'. But it renders them as the smallest text and smallest tap targets in the app, which inverts their importance.
differentiators: Show the working. Every person's figure expands into the arithmetic that produced it, and every total carries a visible reconciliation ('4 shares · $118.40 · exactly the bill'). 'The math is wrong' is the number-one 1-star theme against tricount, Splid and Tab, and none of them can open the box because their maths happens on a server. Ours is integer-cent, largest-remainder and unit-tested, we are the only app in the category that can afford to be audited, and in a category built on social trust, auditability beats every feature on the Pro list.

Free where they charge, and say so as a list. Itemized by-dish splitting, currency conversion, unlimited expenses, unlimited people, no ads, no countdown, every one of those is a named paid feature at Splitwise, Kittysplit or Settle Up. Put the negative-space list exactly where a competitor puts a pricing table. It costs us nothing and is structurally uncopyable by anyone with a payroll.

Nobody else has to install anything, sign up for anything, or be findable. The link and the QR carry the whole split. Kittysplit has proven the demand for this and still gates the tenth person and the second currency; Splid, Splitwise, Settle Up and Venmo all require every participant to hold an account. The QR should be the primary share action at a restaurant table, it is the only one that works across a table without typing someone's phone number.

Every request answers 'what for'. The single most-upvoted structural complaint in this file is a tricount review titled 'Missing most important feature': you cannot ask for repayment without being able to say what it was for. Make the reason travel with the number, into the expanded transfer, into the copied summary, and into the note field of the Venmo/Cash App deep link. Given the Zelle survey finding that 69% of Gen Z say repayment issues have damaged a relationship, this is not a nicety; it is the emotional core of the product.

Two honest views of settle-up: 'fewest payments' and 'pay who you actually owe'. Minimized settlement is elegant and socially baffling, it routes Sam's money through Priya. Users are explicitly asking for the un-netted view. Offering both, with a one-line explanation of each, turns our best algorithm from a source of suspicion into a source of confidence.

We never touch the money, and that is a promise, not a limitation. No custody, no wallet, no escrow, no card on file, no subscription to cancel, against a leader whose loudest reviews are 'impossible to cancel', 'hidden cancellation' and 'trying to get my money back has been impossible', and a rival owned by a bank that hands you a card on signup. Being unable to charge you is a trust asset; state it in plain words.

Nothing expires, nothing syncs behind your back, nothing gets edited under you. Tab deletes bills after a fortnight; tricount users report groups vanishing; Splitwise users report other members editing their entries. One person holds the split and shares a snapshot, that is a coherent, defensible model rather than a missing feature, and it should be described that way in the UI.

Restaurant-table ergonomics as the primary case, not the mobile fallback. Dim room, one hand, a phone held at arm's length so three people can see it, everyone waiting, possibly no signal in the basement of the restaurant. That dictates: the per-person amount as the largest object on screen, 44px minimum on every control including the payment links and the item chips, no landscape lock (Plates' worst 1-star), no hover-only affordances, and a working offline install. 'Turn your Wi-Fi off, it still works' is a claim only we can invite.

Fast manual entry as a deliberate answer to broken OCR. Tab's reviews show scanning is worse than typing when it misses 13 of 15 items and invents prices. Make eight items in thirty seconds the design target, amount field autofocused, numeric keypad, Enter commits and advances, running subtotal live, item name optional, and explain in one line why there is no camera: a scanner means an upload, and an upload means your receipt on somebody's server.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: The category is teal-green and mint. Splitwise owns #1CC29F, Cash App owns green, Venmo owns a bright cyan-blue, PayPal owns navy-and-cyan, and the long tail of Splitwise clones (splitty, fairshare, spliit, hipposplit, settlify, GoodShare, SplitterUp, and the dozens of SEO blogs currently ranking for 'Splitwise alternative') all reach for the same mint-on-white fintech palette with a rounded card stack and a big coloured balance pill. The standard layout: a marketing hero with a phone mockup, an avatar row, a category-icon chip on every expense row, a green/red balance summary at the top, a floating '+' FAB in the bottom-right thumb zone, and, on the free tiers, an interstitial ad or an Instagram-Stories-style upsell screen wedged between you and the add button. Dated tells in 2026: mint-to-blue gradient buttons, cartoon-flat illustrations of diverse friends at a table, coin and piggy-bank iconography, a FAB, an avatar circle with initials on every row, drop-shadowed floating cards on a grey #F7F8FA ground, and a celebratory confetti animation on 'all settled'. What reads as current: content-first pages that show the working surface with no landing preamble; near-flat, high-contrast neutral surfaces; one accent used for state rather than decoration; typographic hierarchy carried by size and weight rather than colour; real dark mode; and, specific to money, tabular-lining numerals with aligned decimal points, which almost nothing in this category bothers with and which instantly reads as competent. The most important convention to break: in this category the brand colour is usually also the balance colour, so 'you owe' green and 'brand' green fight. Ours must not.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: Two moments, and they are not the same. The first is the restaurant table: the check has landed, six people are half-standing, phones are out, one person has volunteered to work it out and everyone is watching them. It is dim, it is noisy, the phone is held at arm's length so two other people can read it, and the social cost of getting it wrong or taking too long is high, this person wants to be finished, not delighted. The second is three days after a trip: someone is alone on a sofa with a folder of receipts, reconstructing a week, and dreading the group-chat message they are about to send. That second moment carries real weight, a July 2026 Zelle survey of 1,000 US consumers reported that 46% of Gen Z currently owe friends or family over $1,000, 47% have gone into debt covering group expenses expecting repayment, 82% feel stress or anxiety about owing money, 69% say repayment issues have affected a friendship or relationship, and 20% have muted a group chat to avoid it. A separate consumer survey found 43.6% have experienced tension when splitting a bill. So the design job is not 'make finance fun'; it is to make the number feel unarguable so the awkward message can be sent without a fight. That dictates: the per-person amount is the largest object on screen and set in tabular numerals; the arithmetic behind it is one tap away and never hidden; nothing animates, celebrates, or congratulates; body text 16px minimum and result figures far larger; 44px targets everywhere including the payment links, because the app is used one-handed while standing; no colour-only meaning, since 'owes' vs 'owed' must survive a dim room, a cracked screen and a colourblind reader; no destructive action without undo, because deleting the wrong item in front of five people is the app's worst possible failure; and absolutely nothing may ever appear over the add-expense control, because that is exactly where every competitor puts its ad. The register is a good waiter with a calculator: quick, exact, unembarrassed about money, and gone before you notice.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: unarguable, exact, calm, plain-spoken, quick, grown-up, receipt-like

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Deep ledger-navy ink, OKLCH hue ≈ 240 (a true blue, not a cyan), chroma ≈ 0.09 to 0.10, taken noticeably darker in value than the current accent, sitting on WARM receipt cream rather than the current cool pale-cyan canvas. Green and red are demoted out of the brand role entirely and reserved exclusively for balance polarity (owed / owing), with a non-colour signal alongside them.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Four forces, in order of weight. (1) FUNCTION, which decides it. This app's two most important colours are already spoken for: --pos green means 'you're owed / settled' and --neg rose means 'you owe'. Any brand accent in the green or red families competes with the only two colours in the UI that carry meaning. That rules out the entire money-green convention and the whole warm-red arc, and it is a stronger argument than novelty. (2) CATEGORY. The category is teal-green: Splitwise is #1CC29F, Cash App is green, Venmo is a bright cyan-blue, and every Splitwise-alternative clone in the current SERP uses mint-on-white. Our shipped accent is #2290a9 on a #eefafd canvas (index.html:40 and :50, with manifest theme_color #00758d), a teal-cyan on pale cyan. That is close enough to Splitwise's family to read as a clone in a category currently flooded with literal clones, and it is the single most consequential mistake in the existing build. (3) PORTFOLIO. skins.mjs puts bill-splitter at hue 218 / chroma 0.10 / paper cool, wedged exactly between scan-to-pdf (202, cool, grid) and pill-schedule (234, cool, plain), three cool-paper apps inside a 32° arc, and the generated accent proves the point by coming out teal rather than the 'steady slate-blue' the note promises. Moving to hue 240 alone is not enough separation from pill-schedule at 234, so the decisive lever is the one skins.mjs itself names as biggest after hue: paper temperature. Flip bill-splitter from cool to WARM. There is currently no app in the portfolio combining warm paper with a genuinely chromatic blue, the only warm cool-hue apps are caregiver-log (250, chroma 0.035, near-grey) and signature-maker (264, chroma 0.022, near-achromatic), both essentially neutral, so a 0.095-chroma navy on cream is 3 to 4× their saturation and cannot be confused with either. Against pill-schedule the separation is temperature (cream vs cool-tinted glass), value (deep ink vs clear mid-blue) and scale (pill-schedule runs 14% larger type). (4) MEANING. Navy ink on warm paper is a receipt, a ledger, a bank statement, a paper check, 'money apps earn trust by being boring' is the right instinct in skins.mjs and this is what it actually looks like. White paper also gives per-person amount cards somewhere to sit, which the current pale-cyan ground does not. Practically: set hue ≈ 240, chroma ≈ 0.095, paper 'warm', keep voice 'technical' and r:12, and consider texture 'rule' (a single accent hairline under the header) over the current 'none' to pick up the ledger register without adding noise. Add tabular-lining numerals (font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums lining-nums) to every money figure, in a column of amounts this reads as competence more than any hue choice will. CONFLICT TO RESOLVE BEFORE BUILD: the pdf-tools research recommends 'deep indigo-navy ink on warm bone' as well. If both are adopted, push them apart on hue, bill-splitter takes the true blue at 240 with a cream (yellow-warm) paper; pdf-tools should keep its violet lean at 276 to 285 with a greyer bone. Do not ship both at the same hue.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Splitwise's #1CC29F and the whole mint/teal/spring-green family, it is the category's default, it is what every clone in the SERP is already wearing, and it collides with our own --pos semantic. Money-green of any kind in a brand role, for the same reason. Red, rose and orange-red in a brand role, they collide with --neg, and in a money app a red-tinted primary button reads as a warning. The current pale-cyan canvas #eefafd and accent #2290a9: cyan is where the category and three of our own apps already live, and the canvas leaves white result cards floating with no contrast. Venmo's bright cyan-blue and the mint→blue gradient button, which is the single most dated tell in fintech. Generic SaaS mid-blue #2563EB, team-parent already owns royal blue at 258/0.15. Any dark-first 'crypto' look: near-black ground with neon accents reads as speculative finance and is exactly wrong for a dinner bill. A floating accent-coloured FAB in the bottom-right thumb zone, it is the category's convention and it is where competitors put their upsell, so it is the one silhouette we should not share. And never let colour alone carry 'owes' vs 'owed': every balance needs an explicit sign or word as well as a hue, and every selected item-chip needs a checkmark as well as a fill (our chips currently signal selection by fill colour only, index.html:2091 renderItems).

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with the strongest evidence in this file being primary and verbatim. METHOD: WebSearch was available and used, supplemented by direct WebFetch. The best source by far was Apple's public customer-reviews RSS endpoint (itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=<trackId>/sortBy=mostRecent/json), which returned genuine 1 to 3 star reviews with reviewer handles for Splitwise (458023433), tricount (349866256), Splid (991473495), Tab (595068606) and Plates (669801762). Every quoted review in this document came from that feed and is verbatim or near-verbatim; none is invented. HIGH CONFIDENCE: Splitwise's Pro feature list including 'Itemization', 'Currency conversion' and 'Receipt scanning' as paid (splitwise.com/pro, fetched directly); Splitwise's own knowledgebase confirming the daily free-tier expense limit and suggesting you ask 'a friend to add the expenses on your behalf' (feedback.splitwise.com); Splitwise's App Store IAP price ladder $2.99 / $3.99 / $4.99 / $29.99 / $39.99 and its App Privacy declaration linking Name, Email, Phone Number and Coarse Location to the user (apps.apple.com listing, fetched directly); App Store ratings and rating counts for all nine apps (iTunes Search API, fetched directly, Splitwise 3.95/26,928; tricount 4.875/6,616; Splid 4.91/3,901; Settle Up 4.82/1,687; Tab 4.22/1,136; Plates 4.34/922); Settle Up's fullscreen ad 'after every 3rd expense added' and the Instagram-Stories-style promo screen (Step Up Labs' own Medium post by the developer); Kittysplit's free-to-9-people limit and ~€3 one-time per-group upgrade covering 10+ members, multi-currency and receipt uploads (kittysplit.com's own comparison page); Venmo Groups launched Nov 2023, 32 people per group, no paywall (TechCrunch and PaymentsJournal); the Zelle-commissioned July 2026 survey figures (Fortune, 27 July 2026, reporting two online surveys of 1,000 US consumers 18+ plus 1,000 Zelle super-users). HIGHEST CONFIDENCE OF ALL: every claim about our own build. I read /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps/bill-splitter/index.html directly (2,657 lines as of this session, note the file grew mid-session, so line numbers in the older bill-splitter.audit.json no longer match; the numbers cited here are current). Verified by reading the source: no settlement/payment record type in sanitizeState; no date, category or note field on an expense; JSON-only export; no Print button despite two @media print blocks; dinner mode has no percentage or exact-amount split and no currency control; settle-up renders only the minimized transfer set; --accent:#2290a9 on --canvas:#eefafd with manifest theme_color #00758d. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE: the exact Splitwise daily cap. Splitwise itself publishes no number; reviewers say 3 ('limited to 3 entries per day', 'a daily limit of 3 expenses'), one says 4, aggregator blogs say 2 to 5. Treat as 'roughly 3 per day, undisclosed and subject to change', never as an official figure. Splitwise Pro's headline price of $39.99/yr and $4.99/mo is inferred by matching the App Store IAP ladder against secondary sources; splitwise.com/pro does not print a price. Settle Up's Premium prices are NOT verified, the developer's post gives no figures. Splitwise brand colour #1CC29F comes from brand-colour aggregator sites; brandfetch.com returned 403 and I did not confirm it from Splitwise's own assets, so treat the hex as indicative and the 'teal-green' characterisation as certain. NOT VERIFIED: Reddit is blocked in this environment (www.reddit.com refused both HTML and .json), so there is no first-hand Reddit sentiment here, the Reddit-flavoured claims in the round-up blogs were not usable and were excluded. Trustpilot returned 403, so the widely-repeated '1.8/5, 65% one-star' Splitwise Trustpilot figure is UNVERIFIED and deliberately not stated as fact anywhere above. Google Play reviews were not readable. A large share of the SERP for every query in this category is competitor-owned content marketing (splitty, spliit.pro, split-circle, tetras, settlify, goodshare, splitterup, nomadcrew, areweeven, usefairsplit, hipposplit, niptao, flatmateflow, donget), all of which exist to sell a Splitwise alternative; none of their numbers are quoted here as evidence, only as pointers to primary sources. tricount's group-deletion complaints were surfaced through search snippets of bunq help-centre threads I did not read in full, treat as directional. Finally, all iOS review evidence is US App Store and self-selecting: people write reviews when angry, so these quotes are reliable as an inventory of what goes wrong, not as a measure of how often it does.
